extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), and USPTO examiners
extracted.subtask_short: operability and enablement in patent appeals
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary rules used by the USPTO, PTAB, and Federal Circuit to evaluate patent claims for utility/operability (§101), enablement/written description/indefiniteness (§112), and related subject-matter questions. Focuses on when skepticism, experimental verification, and claim-scope limits are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility/Operability (35 U.S.C. § 101)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention must be a 'useful invention' and operative; claims that are inoperative or lack credible utility can be rejected under § 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An examiner may reject claims as inoperative when the asserted results lack credibility (the Board described the invention as of an 'incredible nature'). Claims requiring means for accomplishing an unattainable result are invalid under § 101 or § 112 (see Raytheon Co. v. Roper; Milligan). Example: claims asserting weight/temperature/pH changes in an isolated target via a remote manipuation can be rejected as lacking utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement (35 U.S.C. § 112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to practice the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement requires adequate disclosure, cogent explanation of mechanisms, and verifiable test data; bare, non-reproducible experimental reports or speculative assertions fail enablement. The examiner/Board may reasonably require experimental verification and sufficient detail of sources, detecting methods, and parameters to permit practice of the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description Requirement (35 U.S.C. § 112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must demonstrate possession of the claimed invention and support the full scope of the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims will be rejected when the specification fails to describe the claimed subject matter with sufficient detail to show the inventor possessed it. The Board affirmed rejections where the specification did not provide a cogent explanation or sufficient examples to support broad claim scope (written description rejections in the ’739 and ’830 applications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness / Particularity of Claim Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must have the requisite particularity and distinctness; limitations must be sufficiently definite to inform those skilled in the art of the claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of particularity in structural or functional limitations (e.g., 'source' and 'container' described so generally that any known or unknown photon/magnetic pulse generator would suffice) supports indefiniteness or § 101 rejection for lack of a practical application (the Board found such limitations lacked the particularity necessary to qualify as a machine/transformation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of Proof / Prima Facie Case
rubrics_metrics.description: On examination the PTO bears the initial burden of presenting a prima facie case of unpatentability; if met, the applicant must rebut, but the ultimate burden of persuasion remains with the PTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must base rejections on evidence, prior art, knowledge, and analytic reasoning, not mere speculation. If the PTO meets the prima facie showing, the applicant must provide evidence and argument to rebut. Precedent: In re Piasecki, In re Duvi, In re Oetiker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incredible or Implausible-Invention Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO may establish grounds to doubt asserted utility when the written description suggests an inherently unbelievable undertaking or implausible scientific principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an invention appears to contradict established science or ordinary experience, the PTO can require proof of utility/operability (see In re Cortright; In re Brana). The Board may characterize the invention as 'incredible' and sustain rejections absent convincing supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightened Evidentiary Standard for Departures from Scientific Consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claimed invention departs from conventional scientific understanding, a heightened requirement for reproducible experimental verification and convincing evidence may be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO and Board may reasonably demand reproducibility, cogent mechanisms, verifiable test data, and potentially peer recognition before crediting extraordinary claims. The opinion states that concepts that 'strain scientific principles are properly held to a heightened standard, typically measured by reproducibility of results.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption / Claim Scope Must Be Commensurate With Contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim scope must not preempt future developments beyond the applicant's demonstrated contribution to the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even assuming some demonstrated embodiments, claims that 'far exceed' the applicant's contribution and would preempt future developments can be rejected (Board's concern that claim 5's scope 'would far exceed Appellants' contribution to the art—preempting the future before it has arrived').

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial Exceptions to Patentable Subject Matter (Natural Phenomena)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to natural phenomena or natural laws are judicial exceptions to patentable subject matter and require additional elements to show a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An examiner may view phenomena (e.g., 'generating quantum entanglements' as a natural phenomenon) as unpatentable absent particularized machines, transformations, or useful applications. Lack of particularity or usefulness of the asserted application supports sustaining a § 101 rejection (as in the ’739 Board opinion adopting the Examiner's analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Scientific Principles and Evidence in Examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may rely on established scientific principles and available evidence to assess credibility, operability, and compliance with patentability requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion cites examiners invoking conservation of mass and thermodynamics (e.g., 'violates the first law of thermodynamics') as bases to doubt asserted results; absence of known scientific principles explaining how the invention could operate and lack of verifiable data weigh against the applicant. The PTO should ground rejections in analytic reasoning and evidence rather than unsupported skepticism.
